stem: A43-year-old man presents to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of weight gain of 15 kg over the past 3 months. He has hypertension and has been told by his General Practitioner that he has pre-diabetes. His blood pressure is 152/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 35 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate 35 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
explanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with Cushing syndrome given the weight gain,hypertension, pre- diabetes and metabolic alkalosis on blood testing. The 3×24-hour urinary free cortisol test is the most appropriate initial screening test. Where patients can not comply with a urine testing regimen, other options include a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test or a midnight cortisol. If cortisol secretion is significantly increased, adrenocorticotrophic hormone(ACTH) should be measured in an attempt to differentiate between an underlying adrenal adenoma as the underlying cause and pituitary or ectopic ACTH production. Cushing Syndrome Media explanations.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic with gradually worsening peripheral oedema over the past 6months. She is usually well and her only medication is ramipril for idiopathic hypertension. Her blood pressure is 153/82 mmHg and heart rate 73 bpm and regular. There is pitting oedema affecting both lower Limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 119 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 249×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 149μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 24 g/l 35-45 g/l Renal biopsy Thickened capillary walls with subepithelial deposits Urine Protein 3+ blood negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Rituximab is recommended by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes guidelines as the most appropriate option in patients with idiopathic membranous nephropathy at a moderate risk of progression. Approximately two-thirds of patients with membranous nephropathy gain at least partial remission from proteinuria. In those who fail to gain benefit from proteinuria, a calcineurin inhibitor and prednisolone are added. Cyclophosphamide is usually reserved for those who continue to deteriorate despite anti-B-cell therapy. Media explanations.

stem: A 64-year-old man who has hypertension and type Il diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with a hot, swollen erythematous right knee, which he says is too painful to bend. He takes several medications including bendroflumethiazide, ramipril, metformin and sitagliptin. His right knee is swollen and erythematous, and he has psoriasis affecting his scalp and elbows. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 80×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 109 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 45 mg/L 10 mg/l Urate 0.58 mmol/L 0.24-0.51 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Gout diagnosis here. A monoarthritis with a modest elevation in C-reactive protein and elevated plasma urate is consistent with the diagnosis. Given the medical history of diabetes, a knee aspiration to exclude septic arthritis and confirm the diagnosis of gout should be considered. Given the medical history of hypertension, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are not the first-choice option for treatment of acute gout. Colchicine could be considered. Gout Media explanations.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with active lupus presents the Haematology Clinic with worsening shortness of breath and lethargy over the past few days. She is pale, her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and heart rate is 103 bpm and regular.Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 83 g/L 115-155 g/l White cell count 6.8×10/L 4-11×10/l Platelets 140×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Which of the following is the most useful investigation for the patient's anaemia?
explanation: This patient most probably has autoimmune haemolytic anaemia due to an antibody formed as a result of the active lupus. The best way to screen for antibodies that cause haemolysis is using the direct antiglobulin test. Red cells are washed to remove unbound antibodies and are then incubated with anti-human globulin. If the cells agglutinate, then the test is positive and the haemolysis is related to anti-red blood cell antibodies. Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia Media explanations.

stem: A 57-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic with gradually worsening peripheral oedema and a rise in her serum creatinine over the past 6 months. She has taken methotrexate and intermittent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents for the past 12 years for rheumatoid arthritis. Her blood pressure is 149/92 mmHg and heart rate 78 bpm and regular. There is peripheral oedema of both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 108 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count 8.1×10/L 4-11×109/L (WCC) Platelets (PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35-45 g/l Renal ultrasound Increased echogenicity of both kidneys with prominent medullary pyramids Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Amyloid A amyloidosis is associated with chronic inflammatory disorders including rheumatoid arthritis, especially as in this patient in whom the disease has continued for many years. Deposition occurs primarily within the kidney and accounts for this patient's presentation with probable nephrotic range proteinuria and increased kidney echogenicity. Treating the underlying inflammatory condition is crucial to prevent amyloid progression. Amyloidosis Media explanations.

stem: A 24-year-old man who has recently started sodium valproate for epilepsy presents to the Emergency Department with a severe generalised erythematous blistering rash and multiple ulcers affecting his mucous membranes. He has had flu-like symptoms for the past two days, which appeared at the same time as the rash. Examination reveals generalised erythema with small vesicles and de-roofed blisters and multiple ulcers in the mouth. There is bilateral conjunctival injection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is rarely seen in association with sodium valproate therapy and presents with flu-like symptoms, and a generalised erythematous rash with ulceration including of the mucous membranes. It necessitates immediate discontinuation of the causative medication. Patients require supportive therapy. Corticosteroid use is controversial, with limited evidence of benefit, and other immunomodulatory intervention has been used only in small studies. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is of particular concern in patients of Han Chinese origin who are prescribed carbamazepine, an alternative antiepileptic medication. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 8, blood pressure 100/80 mmHg and heart rate 94 bpm and regular. There is a short run of ventricular tachycardia as you are examining her. stem: A 33-year-old woman with bipolar disorder presents to the Endocrine Clinic with polyuria and polydipsia. Current medication includes lithium carbonate 600 mg twice daily and naproxen, which she has been taking for 2-3 months because of a knee injury. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 135 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 12.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 195×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 3.6mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 135μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is seen as a result of chronic lithium use, particularly when levels are too high. Co-prescription of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) is recognised to elevate lithium levels and may well be responsible for the presentation seen here. The isolated elevated white count is seen as a result of chronic lithium use. Lithium should be discontinued if possible and the patient switched to an alternative mood stabiliser, such as sodium valproate. In the event that her symptoms of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus persist once lithium has been discontinued, then a thiazide diuretic used in combination with an NSAID is the pharmacological intervention of choice. Lithium Toxicity Media explanations.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with tiredness, loss of libido and milk leakage on minimal nipple stimulation. Her optician has also noted loss of peripheral vision on visual field testing. Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary finds macroadenoma with pressure on the optic chiasma. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.7 IU/L 0.5-4.5 IU/L Prolactin 8950 IU/L 700 IU/L
explanation: Dopamine agonists are the initial therapy of choice for both micro-and macroprolactinoma. In patients with a large tumour, the prolactinoma can be successfully treated as a single intervention, or at the very least reduce tumour size and reduce the risk of haemorrhage at the point of surgical intervention. Cabergoline is usually given at a dose of 0.25 or 0.5 mg twice weekly. Prolactinoma Media explanations.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted with shortness of breath and a worsening cough over the past 48 hours. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. There is poor air entry and bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Her arterial blood gas results are shown below. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value PO 7.6kPa 10-13 kPa PCO 8.4 kPa 4.7-6.0kPa pH HCO- 35 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Which of the following best describes her blood gas picture?
explanation: This patient's clinical picture is consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD), which over time leads to a compensated respiratory acidosis picture on blood gas testing. She is carbon dioxide retaining with low oxygen, and there is conservation of serum bicarbonate to maintain the pH in the normal range. This shows that the patient has had significant pulmonary dysfunction for some time. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Media explanations.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner after returning from a teaching trip to Thailand with severe intermittent fevers, abdominal pain,nausea and vomiting. Her temperature is 38.9°℃, blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg and heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. She has generalised abdominal tenderness, but her abdomen is soft with active bowel sounds. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 89 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count 8.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 98×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 133 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 118μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thick and thin film Vivax malaria identified Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: Malaria Media explanations Artemether and lumefantrine combination therapy is the initial intervention of choice for non-falciparum.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with dehydration and a urinary tract infection. A 1-litre bolus of 0.9% saline is given intravenously. Which of the following is the likely increase in intravascular volume?
explanation: Around 20% to 25% of isotonic fluid administered remains in the intravascular space followed by a further increase due to increase in osmolality of the extracellular fluid, so, if 1 litre is given, it's expected that around 200-250 ml remains.

stem: A72-year-old woman is taken to the operating theatre because of suspected ischaemic colitis. The terminal ileum is found to be ischaemic. Which of the following is the blood supply to the terminal ileum?
explanation: The ileocolic artery supplies blood to the terminal ileum and the appendix. It is the most inferior branch of the superior mesenteric artery. It terminates in the right iliac fossa by dividing into superior and inferior branches. It is the inferior branch that primarily supplies the appendix and terminal ileum.

stem: A73-year-old man is admitted to the Palliative Care Ward with intractable nausea and vomiting. He has pancreatic carcinoma and Parkinson's disease for which he takes three medications. He is mildly jaundiced and tender in the epigastrium on palpation. He has active bowel sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice of antiemetic for the patient?
explanation: Ondansetron is a 5-hydroxytryptamine-3 receptor antagonist with centrally acting antiemetic properties. It is not a dopamine antagonist, which means that it can be used safely in patients with Parkinson's disease. Ondansetron may cause Q-T prolongation, meaning that caution is advised when it is prescribed with other drugs that may prolong the Q-T interval. Q.

stem: A49-year-old man with type ll diabetes presents to General Practitioner for review. His glycated haemoglobin is still elevated at 58 mmol/mol. Current medication is metformin 1 g twice daily. It is decided to start him on sitagliptin. Which of the following is the mode of action of sitagliptin?
explanation: Dipeptidyl peptidase 4 is an enzyme that breaks down incretin hormones such as glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon. By interfering with the breakdown of natural GLP-1, sitagliptin enhances the incretin effect and reduces blood glucose. It has modest positive effects on weight. Unlike sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors, it does not significantly improve cardiovascular outcomes. Q.

stem: A19-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after a collapse. According to her mother she is not eating and has frequent episodes of vomiting. Her body mass index is 15 kg/m.Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and her electrocardiogram reveals T-wave inversion and prominent U waves. What is the most likely cause of the electrocardiogram appearance?
explanation: This patient has a likely diagnosis of an eating disorder and is significantly underweight with symptoms of vomiting. The electrocardiogram(ECG)changes with T-wave inversion and the presence of U waves are consistent with hypokalaemia and/or hypomagnesaemia. Once hypokalaemia has been confirmed, then intravenous potassium replacement is recommended; magnesium levels should also be checked and replaced appropriately. Cardiac monitoring is recommended until potassium levels rise, given the ECG findings here. Q.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has multiple joint pains and a photosensitive rash, particularly affecting her face and upper arms. Past medical history includes two previous miscarriages and an unprovoked left lower limb deep venous thrombosis some two years ago. An erythematous rash affecting the face and synovitis affecting the fingers, wrists, elbows, knees and ankles is confirmed. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation: Anti-double-stranded (ds)DNA antibodies are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) which fits with the picture seen here of synovitis, a photosensitive rash, previous deep vein thrombosis and miscarriages. Between 70% and 98% of patients with SLE are thought to test positive for anti-dsDNA antibodies. Evaluation of renal function will help drive the choice of therapy for this patient;renal disease skews disease-modifying therapy more towards mycophenolate. Predominant joint and skin disease drives the use of hydroxychloroquine. Q.

stem: A19-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic after collapsing during an argument with his girlfriend. He admits to episodes of palpitations and one episode of fainting after he went running. He is usually fit and well and takes no regular medication. His blood pressure is 123/82mmHg and heart rate is 67 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm,QT interval 480 ms(normal value450 ms). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has a QT interval450 ms.In the presence of two episodes of collapse associated with sympathetic stimulation (exercise and emotion), a diagnosis of long QT syndrome is suspected. Beta- blockers are the medical intervention of choice. In high-risk patients who have already suffered an episode of collapse/cardiac arrest, an implantable cardioverter defibrillator should be considered. Q.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic for the second time in the past 12 months. She is requesting a colonoscopy. She has had a previous colonoscopy and one upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. She is concerned that she may have colon cancer because her grandfather passed away from the disease around 18months ago. She reports having intermittent abdominal bloating. All her investigations, including a range of blood tests, have been normal so far. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Illness anxiety is characterised by excessive rumination about a serious illness(in this case colon cancer), even in the face of evidence against there being a significant underlying health problem. The trigger here has been the death of her grandfather due to colon cancer. Unfortunately, continuing to request more investigations is likely to reinforce her behaviour. Cognitive behavioural therapy is the preferred intervention, helping patients to identify their fears and beliefs about underlying illness and develop strategies to modify these. Q.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with a5kg weight gain in 6 months, tiredness, hair loss and depressive thoughts. Examination reveals a smooth enlarged goitre. Thyroid-stimulating hormone test results are 13.2 mU/L(normal value 0.5-4.5 mU/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is associated with a smooth goitre related to lymphocytic thyroid infiltration and hypothyroidism. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism and occurs most commonly in women aged 30-50 years. Treatment with thyroxine is required; it is usually commenced at a dose of 50 μg and uptitrated. Over the longer term, Hashimoto's thyroiditis is associated with an increased risk of thyroid lymphoma. Q.

stem: A 45-year-old man who has moved to the United Kingdom from Egypt presents to the Rheumatology Clinic. He has suffered recurrent anterior uveitis, orogenital ulceration and erythema nodosum affecting both shins. He suffered a deep vein thrombosis affecting the left lower limb one year ago. Which human leukocyte antigen subtype is most associated with his presentation?
explanation: This patient's clinical presentation of anterior uveitis, orogenital ulceration and erythema nodosum, with a previous deep vein thrombosis, is highly suggestive of Bechet's disease. Human leukocyte antigen-B51 is characteristically associated with Bechet's disease, which has a greater incidence in people of Mediterranean origin. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after a collapse while attending university. According to her flatmates, she does not eat and obsessively exercises. She has a past medical history of self-harming, which resolved after a prolonged course of psychotherapy. Her body mass index is 16 kg/m. She has fine hairs over her arms and legs. Which of the following is the best way to manage her eating disorder?
explanation: This patient obsessively exercises and has a past history of mental illness and there are features of anorexia nervosa, including an extremely low body mass index and fine hairs over her arms and legs. Specialist eating disorder-focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the intervention of choice, which typically involves 40 sessions over 40 weeks, beginning at more than one per week. Other options include a Maudsley-designed eating disorder therapy programme known as MANTRA and specialist support clinical management. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection for three days. He has developed a morbiliform rash that began over the face and has now spread to involve the upper torso. His temperature is 38.9℃,and he has obvious conjunctivitis. Examination of the buccal mucosa reveals a number of small red spots, each with a white fleck at the centre. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The three days of coryzal symptoms followed by a morbilliform rash that begins on the face and spreads distally, coupled with the presence of Koplik's spots affecting the buccal mucosa, are typical of a diagnosis of measles. Immunisation rates have fallen off in recent years and it's possible that his parents may have refused to have him immunised. Treatment is supportive, and complications include otitis media, pneumonitis and,in 1 in 1000 cases, acute demyelinating encephalitis. Q.
