stem: A73-year-old man with type ll diabetes is admitted to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset right hemiplegia and a left third nerve palsy. Which of the following cerebral arteries is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation: This patient has Weber's syndrome, characterised by ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia. It is most commonly caused by occlusion of a branch of the posterior cerebral artery which leads to a midbrain infarction. Magnetic resonance imaging is the most sensitive way to detect any underlying infarction. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A19-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner after being diagnosed with factor V Leiden mutation after suffering an extensive, left leg, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. What is the cause of an increased risk of thrombosis in this patient?
explanation: The factor V Leiden mutation leads to activated protein C resistance. Activated protein C normally cleaves coagulation factor V, but in those with the Leiden mutation this doesn't happen. The role of factor V is to act as a cofactor to allow factor Xa to activate prothrombin, resulting in formation of thrombin. Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to form fibrin, which makes up the dense network found within a clot. In patients with the factor Leiden mutation, factor V is not properly inactivated, which can cause a clot to grow out of control. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with two previous admissions to an Intensive Therapy Unit is brought by ambulance to the Emergency Department with a severe exacerbation of asthma. She has taken 40 mg oral prednisolone each day for the past 2 days. Review after 30 minutes of continuous salbutamol nebulisers reveals a peak flow of 210 L/min (510 predicted). Which of the following is the most useful next step?
explanation: This patient's peak flow has failed to recover to50% of predicted despite back-to-back nebulisers. At this point magnesium is indicated according to British Thoracic Society/Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network guidelines. It is delivered intravenously at a dose of 1.2-2 g delivered over 20 min. Although evidence from a meta-analysis has proved equivocal, it included significant numbers of patients with peak respiratory flow rate50% of predicted. A sub-analysis of the most severe patients indicated a probable benefit for magnesium. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A19-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with Epstein-Barr virus(EBV) infection. He has splenic tenderness on palpation of the abdomen. He plays professional rugby. He asks how long he needs to wait before he can return to contact sports. How long does it take before the risk of splenic rupture is back to normal levels?
explanation: NICE guidelines currently recommend avoidance of contact sports for the first four weeks after diagnosis. Although research has suggested a longer period of time and potential follow-up USS scans to assess risk, this is not currently guidance. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the Transient lschaemic Attack Clinic following an episode of dysphasia and left-arm weakness that lasted for 4 hours. He has hypertension and type ll diabetes mellitus. His blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg and heart rate 76 bpm(atrial fibrillation). His chest is clear and his body mass index 24 mg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most appropriate intervention for his atrial fibrillation?
explanation: This patient has significant risk factors for a further transient ischaemic attack,with hypertension,type ll diabetes and atrial fibrillation. As such he should be treated with a direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban. A dose of 5mg twice daily is usual. It can be reduced to 2.5mg where the patient is aged80 years and has renal impairment or low body weight. The ventricular rate does not suggest an acute need for rate control. Atrial Fibrillation explanations.

stem: A19-year-old man who has neurofibromatosis type 2 is reviewed in the Neurology Clinic because of bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals bilateral cerebellopontine angle tumours affecting the vestibular nerve. Which of the following is the most likely composition of these tumours?
explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 2(NF2) is associated with the development of bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Schwann cells, which make up schwannomas, are a subset of glial cells that are thought to support nerve regeneration. In NF2, the development of the tumours is thought to be due to a mutation in merlin, a tumour- suppressor protein also known as neurofibromin 2.Neurofibromatosis type 2(NF2) makes up around 3% of cases of neurofibromatosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a fracture of the left humerus sustained when she was rotating her arm to open a door. She has no medical illnesses. The X-ray is suggestive of a pathological fracture due to a bony metastasis. Which of the following is the most likely site of her primary tumour?
explanation: Around 70% of breast cancers metastasise to bone.In this case, it's quite possible that a small breast cancer, which the patient has been unable to detect herself, has already metastasised. The absence of any chest symptoms and the lack of any neck masses count against both lung and thyroid cancers as potential alternative causes of this patient's fracture.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic complaining of facial erythema and prominent sebaceous glands around the folds of his nose. He says that the problem has got steadily worse over the past 6 months. He drinks 4 pints of beer a day. Examination reveals facial telangiectasias, particularly over the forehead and cheeks. There is erythema and very prominent sebaceous glands over the nasal folds. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Topical azelaic acid 15% has been proven to improve symptoms of rosacea (the diagnosis here) in a Cochrane meta-analysis. Patients may complain of skin irritation that precipitates a switch of medication. Alternatives where there is high-quality evidence to support their use include topical ivermectin, doxycycline, isotretinoin and brimonidine.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with lethargy, night sweats, shortness of breath and haemoptysis, which have steadily increased over the past 3 weeks. She has recently consulted a plastic surgeon because of collapse of the bridge of her nose and trouble with sinusitis. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. There are inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 99 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 182×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 199μmol/ 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following antibodies is characteristic of her condition?
explanation: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis Media explanations This patient has evidence of pulmonary and renal vasculitis and midline sinusitis affecting her nose. The constellation of symptoms raises the possibility of granulomatosis with polyangiitis which is associated with cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA) positivity in up to 90% of cases. Around 90% of patients respond to a combination of high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide to induce remission.

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with back pain, which he says is much worse first thing in the morning and is often so painful that he can hardly get out of bed for the first 2 hours each day. His symptoms have been present for the last 4 months. He has tried naproxen on the advice of his General Practitioner with little relief. His C-reactive protein is elevated at 85mg/L(10 mg/L). Examination reveals limitation of forward and lateral flexion of the lower back. Which of the following is the most useful imaging investigation?
options: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints
Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints
Plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints
explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging is most useful in confirming sacroiliitis in patients with early ankylosing spondylitis. It is more useful than both a plain X-ray and a computed tomography scan in this situation. Changes can drive the selection of patients for early introduction of anti-tumour necrosis factor medication. Magnetic resonance imaging is also of value in late ankylosing spondylitis to detect spinal fracture.

stem: An 18-year-old man is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic having suffered from a haemarthrosis of the right knee after a twisting injury playing football and significant bleeding after wisdom tooth extraction. Physical examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 139 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 76μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Prothrombin time 12 s 11-13.5s Activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s 21-35 s Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Von Willebrand Disease Media explanations von Willebrand's disease (VWD) is associated in 60-80% of cases with a quantitative reduction in levels of von Willebrand's factor (type 1 disease). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and often presents in males as bleeding after dental extraction or orthopaedic injury.von Willebrand's factor binds to factor VIII, preventing its clearance from plasma, and assists in platelet plug formation. It is notable that activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is normal in around half of the patients with vWD.Desmopressin is used in patients with vWD at the time of a procedure because it causes a temporary increase in both factor VIII and von Willebrand's factor.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner complaining that he is frequently tripping over and feels like his left foot is catching. He has had problems with his lumbar spine in the past. Based on the diagnosis of L5 nerve root compression, where is weakness and sensory loss most likely to be found?
options: Weakness of hip flexion and adduction and sensory loss over the upper thigh
Weakness of knee extension and sensory loss over the front and inside of the thigh
Weakness of big toe extension and sensory loss over the big toe
Weakness of ankle plantar flexion only and sensory loss over the lateral foot
Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and sensory loss over the medial knee and shin
explanation: Weakness of big toe extension is characteristic of an L5 nerve root lesion. The L5 nerve root also contributes to the muscles involved in ankle dorsiflexion, although a substantial component of nerve supply to these muscles comes from the L4 root. It is also responsible for sensory supply over the big toe.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Ward complaining of shortness of breath on exercise over the past 6 months.He has no past medical history and takes no regular medication. His blood pressure is 141/82 mmHg and heart rate 68 bpm and regular. His chest is clear and he has no ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 141 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Cardiac Failure Media explanations Angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE)inhibitors or beta-blockers are the initial intervention of choice for the treatment of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. The choice of which agent to start first is dependent on patient status and physician preference. Given that this patient's heart rate is75 bpm it seems reasonable to start the ACE inhibitor first and then add in the beta-blocker as a second intervention. Renal function should be measured 1-2 weeks after starting therapy and after every dose increment.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Emergency Department with a random blood glucose of 22mmol/L. He has suffered from polyuria and polydipsia for several months and had three episodes of candida infection. His father and brother also have diabetes. His body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the patient's hyperglycaemia? Investigations Result Normal value Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Random glucose 23 mmol/L 11.1 mmol/L Fasting glucose (repeated) 7.3 mmol/L 7.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate 27 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Venous pH
explanation: This patient most probably has maturity-onset diabetes of the young(MODY), which is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 alpha MODY is associated with mild fasting hyperglycaemia and marked hyperglycaemia after a glucose challenge, which fits with the picture seen here. This pattern is seen because it is characterised by defective insulin release by beta-cells. Many patients, even 30 years after diagnosis,are still responsive to sulfonylureas and have been able to stop insulin therapy.

stem: A21-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after an overdose of paracetamol. She has had eight episodes of self-harm requiring hospital admission and lacerations to her forearms on multiple occasions over the past five years. She has two children and recently split from a male partner. She hates herself, is always angry and admits that she sometimes acts in a destructive way. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's clinical features fit with a borderline personality disorder, including unstable and intense interpersonal relationships, unstable self-image, a tendency to act rashly and repeated episodes of self- harm. There is emotional instability and chronic feelings of emptiness. Unfortunately, personality disorders may be very resistant to cognitive-behavioural therapy and years of intervention may be required. Mentalisation-based therapy may be of value including group and individual therapy.

stem: A54-year-old man with a history of alcoholism presents to the General Practitioner with haematemesis. He is found on endoscopy to have a large bleeding ulcer affecting the duodenal cap. Which of the following is the blood supply to the duodenal cap?
explanation: The gastroduodenal artery is a terminal branch of the common hepatic artery. It mainly supplies the pylorus of the stomach, proximal duodenum and head of the pancreas. It is close to the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, which makes it one of the most important sources of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner requesting essential vaccinations. He has not been covered as a child because his mother refused to allow him to have them. He is planning to go travelling to South and Central America. He has suffered a serious allergic reaction to egg in the past. Which of the following vaccines must be avoided for this patient?
explanation: Yellow fever vaccine contains significant amounts of egg protein,meaning that in a patient with severe egg allergy it is best avoided. The patient should be given an exemption certificate and advised to minimise time spent in a yellow fever-endemic area.

stem: A19-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department in a state of collapse. She is known to have type l diabetes and has been unwell with symptoms of a cold for the past few days. Her flatmates say that she has had severe nausea and vomiting. Her temperature is 37.8℃, her heart rate is 105 bpm and regular and blood pressure 90/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is generally tender with active bowel sounds. Her respiratory rate is 32 breaths per min. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count 13.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 382×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.6 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate 15 mmol/L 23-30 mmol/L Creatinine 135μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 39 mmol/L 7 mmol/L Which of the following is the most important next step?
explanation: Patients with diabetic ketoacidosis, the probable diagnosis here, may have lost≥5 litres of fluid at the time of presentation. Fluid replacement is essential and the Association of British Clinical Diabetologists guidelines recommend giving 500 ml of 0.9% saline at presentation. Potassium replacement is recommended from when the serum potassium falls to5.5 mmol/L. A fixed-rate insulin regimen rather than a sliding scale is now recommended for control of blood glucose (0.1 U/kg per hour).

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with night sweats, weight loss and a new systolic murmur. He had a hip replacement some 6months earlier. An echocardiogram has demonstrated aortic valve vegetations, and blood cultures demonstrate Streptococcus gallolyticus infection. Which of the following is the most likely origin of the infection?
explanation: Streptococcus bovis endocarditis is seen in both patients with underlying colon cancer and patients with disease of the biliary tree. Where it is identified as the cause of endocarditis, colonoscopy is the most important investigation. Where the colonoscopy fails to identify an underlying cancer, then imaging of the biliary tree should be performed. Infection is associated with both cholangiocarcinoma and ascending cholangitis.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a high fever, dry cough and abdominal pain. He returned a few days earlier from a missionary trip to the Philippines countryside. His temperature is 38.9℃, blood pressure 105/80 mmHg and heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. He has an urticarial rash. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest and he has right upper quadrant pain on palpation of the abdomen. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count 11.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l C-reactive protein 95 mg/l 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Schistosomiasis Media explanations This patient has symptoms consistent with Katayama's fever, which occurs when the cercariae of Schistosoma spp.migrate through the lungs. Fever, shortness of breath and a dry cough are commonly seen features. S. japonicum is the most common cause of Katayama's fever and infection with the schistosomes is thought to occur when patients swim in contaminated water. Stool microscopy and serology are used to confirm the diagnosis, and praziquantel is the intervention of choice. Corticosteroids may also be required to dampen the inflammatory immune response.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with hyperparathyroidism and a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour. Her sister and her father have both suffered from similar problems. Which of the following other tumours is she most likely to have?
explanation: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1(MEN1), the probable diagnosis here, is associated with hyperparathyroidism in which four-gland hyperplasia is often found and pituitary tumours occur, with prolactinoma being the most common subtype. The third finding is a pancreatic endocrine tumour in 70% of patients. Around 60% of pancreatic endocrine tumours are gastrinomas and around 30% are insulinomas. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1(MEN1) is autosomal dominant with a high degree of penetrance. Cutaneous tumours are common in MEN1 with angiofibromas, collagenomas and lipomas all being found.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed in the Genetics Clinic after the development of an osteosarcoma of her right femur. Her brother also suffered from a sarcoma and a sister had early onset breast cancer.
explanation: The presentation here fits with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which carries an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and is associated with a TP53mutation. When TP53 gene expression occurs normally, it functions as a tumour-suppressor gene and mutations reduce the effectiveness of tumour suppression. The syndrome is associated with increased risk of bone and soft-tissue sarcomas and an increased risk of breast cancer.

stem: A76-year-old woman who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to the Nephrology Clinic complaining of urinary incontinence when she laughs or strains to carry heavy objects. She has tried pelvic floor exercises without any improvement in her symptoms. She has a hyperexpanded chest with quiet breath, sounds consistent with COPD. She is obese with a body mass index of 30 kg/m. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Duloxetine is a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. As well as possessing antidepressant properties it has been shown to improve symptoms of stress incontinence. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines support its use, as here, in a patient who has failed to show improvement with pelvic floor exercises and for whom surgical intervention is not an option.

stem: A42-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with frequent headaches and poorly controlled hypertension. She also suffers from sweating and her rings no longer fit on her fingers. Her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg, and she has a prominent lower jaw and macroglossia. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most useful next investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 133 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.2×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 192×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose (fasting) 6.5 mmol/L 7 mmol/L
options: Mixed meal test with growth hormone assay
explanation: Acromegaly Media explanations Insulin growth factor 1(IGF-1) is produced by the liver and has a long half-Life of around 15 hours. It correlates directly with growth hormone levels and is a useful initial investigation in possible acromegaly, the probable diagnosis here. It can be measured as an outpatient test and followed later with an oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone assay. Pituitary imaging is also indicated if IGF-1 levels are raised.

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his flatmates. He developed chickenpox lesions over his upper body a few days earlier and, over the past few days, has started with a dry cough and increased shortness of breath. His temperature is 38.6°℃, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg and heart rate 95 bpm and regular. He has coarse crackles over both lung fields on auscultation. Oxygen saturation is 91% on air. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 149 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 183×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein 67 mg/l 10 mg/l Chest X-ray Bilateral nodular opacities Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Intravenous (aciclovir is the intervention of choice for chickenpox pneumonia, the probable diagnosis here.A dose of 10 mg/kg body weight every 8 hours is recommended. This may need to be reduced in elderly people or obese patients.The drug works by interfering with viral deoxyribonucleic acid(DNA) polymerase by causing chain termination once it has been incorporated into viral DNA. Between 5% and 15% of patients with chickenpox infection may get pulmonary complications, and the rate is significantly increased when primary infection occurs later in life.

stem: A74-year-old woman who is in the terminal stages of breast cancer is reviewed on the Palliative Care Ward. She was admitted with acute renal failure and is now distressed and anxious. She is crying out and shouting that the nursing staff are trying to poison her. Her daughter is very upset because she is hitting out at her. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Haloperidol is the intervention of choice for agitation against a background of delirium in the palliative care and elderly care settings. A dose of 0.5 mg either orally or intramuscularly is recommended by guidelines and this can be repeated every 30 min. If haloperidol is contraindicated, then a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam is the most appropriate alternative.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who has osteoarthritis of both knees comes to the General Practitioner for review. Her pain is not controlled by regular paracetamol and she is requesting further pain relief. Past medical history of note includes peptic ulcer disease related to Helicobacter pyloriand coronary stenting for a left anterior descending lesion 3 years earlier. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for additional pain relief?
explanation: This patient is obese with osteoarthritis pain that is not controlled by regular paracetamol alone. She may benefit further from a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug(NSAID) in controlling her pain, but the previous peptic ulcer disease suggests that, if possible, an NSAID should be given together with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection. As such naproxen and omeprazole in combination is the correct answer here.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who has type l diabetes presents to the General Practitioner complaining of raised red nodular lesions on both shins and on her elbows.Her only medication is insulin and the oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis that is associated with raised red/violet nodular lesions affecting the shins and other extensor surfaces such as the elbows. It is associated with pregnancy, use of the oral contraceptive pill, sarcoidosis and tuberculosis, and fits well with the use of the combined oral contraceptive pill seen here. The rash is likely to resolve if the patient moves to a non-oestrogen-based form of contraception. Non- steroidal anti-inflammatory agents may reduce symptoms.

stem: A45-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner complaining of unilateral throbbing headaches which come on two to three times a month. She says the headaches are usually accompanied by a feeling of nausea and may last for a few hours. Her periods have become lighter over the past few months and they are intermittently missed, but a pregnancy test is negative. Her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg and neurology exam is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has nausea and a unilateral throbbing headache that can last for a few hours. This is consistent with migraine headaches which are often seen in association with hormonal fluctuation in perimenopausal women. Other features apart from nausea include visual disturbance, which may be seen before the onset of the headache. Triptans are the acute intervention of choice for migraine headache, with tricyclic antidepressants an option for long-term migraine prophylaxis.

stem: A 34-year-old man who has type I diabetes attends his General Practitioner for a routine review. He says that he has developed intermittent blurred vision affecting his left eye. Fundoscopy reveals several hard exudates in a circinate pattern affecting the macula of the left eye and dot-and-blot haemorrhages affecting both eyes. His blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg and glycated haemoglobin 54 mmol/mol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: The circinate of hard exudates seen here is suggestive of diabetic macular oedema. This is potentially sight threatening. Focal laser photocoagulation is the most appropriate intervention because it's thought to have the largest efficacy benefit and is accompanied by a large body of safety data. Intravitreal anti-vascularr endothelial growth factor therapy is thought to be less effective and ranibizumab is not endorsed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence because of cost.Intravitreal corticosteroids are thought to have a very small benefit, which is often only temporary.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the Chest Clinic with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy discovered on chest X-ray. She presented to her General Practitioner some 4 weeks earlier with non-specific symptoms of tiredness. Examination is unremarkable apart from some erythematous nodules affecting the shins of both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 42 mg/L 10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sarcoidosis explanations Of cases of sarcoidosis≥50% are thought to be asymptomatic. In this case the presence of erythema nodosum and lethargy as the only symptoms is entirely in keeping with the diagnosis. The small increase in C-reactive protein also fits with the diagnosis. Only around 5% of patients with sarcoidosis have an elevated serum calcium. Although systemic corticosteroids are likely to resolve this patient's erythema nodosum, given that her symptoms are so limited, topical or intralesional steroids may be more appropriate.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner three years after roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. She has been taking regular multivitamin tablets. Which of the following deficiency is the most likely to be seen post-surgery?
explanation: Iron deficiency is common after roux-en-Y bypass surgery and actually gets worse as the postoperative period is extended. Up to year three, some 20% or more of patients are diagnosed with iron deficiency despite supplementation. This is because absorption of iron is significantly impacted by the change of anatomy associated with surgery. Many patients require continuous oral iron supplementation and up to 25% may need intermittent intravenous iron.

stem: A 63-year-old man who suffered a myocardial infarction three months earlier presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He is short of breath on minimal exercise and has suffered two syncopal episodes in the past two weeks. He is currently taking ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide. His blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg and heart rate is 62 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal. His chest is clear although he has swelling of both ankles. Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows right bundle branch block, left axis deviation and QRS 140 ms. Ejection fraction is at 25%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 149 g/L 135-175 g/L White cell count 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 170×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: This patient has bifascicular block and significant heart failure symptoms with an ejection fraction of 25%. He is at risk of progressing to complete heart block and could also benefit from cardiac resynchronisation therapy. As such,the most appropriate next step is to implant a cardiac resynchronisation therapy with a pacemaker device. There is value in switching the ramipril to sacubitril valsartan only after other treatment options have been instituted and there is no value in using ivabradine given that the resting pulse is 62 bpm.

stem: An 18-year-old woman who works in a nursery presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset watery diarrhoea with mucus and blood over the past six hours. Several children and staff at the nursery have had the same symptoms over the last week. She has a 15-mmHg postural drop in blood pressure moving from lying to standing and her heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. She has left-sided abdominal tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Shigella sonneiis highly infectious and spreads rapidly through toddler day-care centres. It leads to acute watery diarrhoea accompanied by mucus or blood and can be associated with postural hypotension where fluid loss is significant. Symptoms generally last for around three days and should resolve spontaneously. Only when symptoms are very severe, or patients immunocompromised, are antibiotics usually considered, with azithromycin being an appropriate option.

stem: A54-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion. He is known to be an alcoholic who drinks 750 ml of whisky a day. He has ophthalmoplegia with an inability to look up and there is horizontal nystagmus. According to his partner, he has been vomiting over the past few days. The nursing staff have checked his blood sugar and found it to be 2.9 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Although traditional teaching suggests that thiamine should always be given first in Wernicke's encephalopathy, the underlying diagnosis here, the patient has significant hypoglycaemia with a blood sugar of 2.9 mmol/L. Intravenous (IV) 20% dextrose is therefore the most appropriate intervention. No cases of worsening Wernicke's encephalopathy have been precipitated by a single bolus of glucose, although a prolonged carbohydrate infusion does worsen symptoms unless it is accompanied by thiamine replacement.

stem: A 34-year-old man with plaque psoriasis presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He wants to know about the cause of his disease. In psoriasis, approximately how long does it take for keratinocytes to transform to anucleate corneocytes?
explanation: Key to the pathogenesis of psoriasis is increased keratinocyte turnover, with a shortening of the time taken to transform from a keratinocyte to an anucleate corneocyte from around 28-30 days to 3 days. Epidermal cells also fail to secrete adequate amounts of lipid, which leads to skin scaling because of loss of integrity of the stratum corneum. There is increased skin vascularisation and infiltration of T cells, in addition to a shortened time for skin cell turnover.

stem: A78-year-old man presents to the Recovery Ward after a left hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. He has had Parkinson's disease for the past 10 years and takes levodopa and ropinirole. He is hitting out at the nursing staff and threatening to fall out of bed. He reports the doctor on call is here to kill him. His temperature is 37.2℃. He refuses to comply with other aspects of the clinical examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?
explanation: Lorazepam is the preferred sedation for patients with delirium occurring against a background of Parkinson's disease. Lorazepam 0.5-1mg intramuscularly can be given in repeated doses up to a total of 3 mg over a 24-hour period. It is preferred to haloperidol because dopamine antagonists can significantly worsen movement disorder in the Parkinson's disease population.

stem: A 25-year-old man dies of cystic fibrosis before he can receive a lung transplant after repeated exacerbations in his last 3 months of life. He undergoes a postmortem examination. Which cell type is increased most in inflammation related to cystic fibrosis?
explanation: Neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, CD4T and cytotoxic T cells are all significantly increased in the airways of patients with cystic fibrosis versus controls, but there is a disproportionate increase in neutrophils in men versus the other cell types. Eosinophils, mast cells and Tlymphocytes are particularly increased in women rather than men.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is treated with a combination of ambrisentan and sildenafil for primary pulmonary hypertension. Which of the following is most likely to be found on cardiovascular assessment?
explanation: Significant pulmonary hypertension (as is likely here given that the patient has been treated with two oral agents) leads to significant back pressure, which in turn leads to tricuspid regurgitation. In time this leads to progressive right atrial dilatation. Right ventricular hypertrophy and a significant increase in pulmonary artery pressures are also seen.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with marked haematuria. She received her latest round of chemotherapy for small-cell lung cancer a few days ago. She is being treated with a combination regimen of ifosfamide and immunotherapy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
explanation: Both cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide form toxic metabolites such as acrolein which can lead to haemorrhagic cystitis. Both drugs are given with Mesna, a sulphonate that forms a conjugate with acrolein and other urotoxic metabolites to render them inactive. Haemorrhagic cystitis is may still be seen, despite co- administration of Mesna.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents to the Recovery Ward after an elective left total knee replacement. He lives alone and usually goes to the local pub for his meals. After 24-hours, he becomes acutely unwell. His blood pressure is 155/100 mmHg and his heart rate 92 bpm and regular. He is sweating, tremulous and hallucinating that there are insects crawling over the bed and up his legs. He refuses to cooperate with a physical examination and lashes out at the doctor with his walking aid. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient is potentially around 48 hours after his last intake of alcohol and the symptoms described here would fit with an episode of delirium tremens, with extreme agitation, signs of sympathetic activation and hallucinations. He is at risk of neurological deterioration, with possible seizures. Chlordiazepoxide can be commenced in 10-mg doses, up to a maximum of 60-100 mg/day. Once symptom control has been reached, a plan can be instituted to reduce the dose over a few days.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with weakness of her left leg. She says it came on suddenly and she is now unable to walk and uses a wheelchair. The symptoms followed distressing news that her father had suffered a stroke. She has no past medical history of note. Physical examination is unremarkable. Reflexes and tone are normal in both lower limbs. When her leftleg is lifted, it falls gradually back down to the bed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's presentation fits well with a conversion disorder in which an individual usually presents with symptoms suggestive of a nervous system disorder. Examples include loss of vision, deafness or,as here, weakness of a limb.There is usually an emotional trigger as here, where the patient's father has suffered a stroke. Symptoms usually resolve spontaneously over a few weeks. When symptoms persist, long-term intervention with cognitive behavioural therapy may be required.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with bipolar disease presents to the General Practitioner complaining of polyuria and polydipsia. Her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most useful next investigation before a water deprivation test? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count 7.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 178×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
explanation: This patient's symptoms are suggestive of diabetes insipidus (DI), which may be nephrogenic and related to Lithium used to treat bipolar disorder. The symptoms may also be associated with psychogenic polydipsia, which is associated with bipolar disorder. Paired urine and plasma osmolality are a useful potential pointer to the diagnosis, with high plasma and low urine osmolality suspicious of DI.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with chronic tiredness and limb weakness. She has never been able to do sports and even has occasional palpitations. Her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg and heart rate 72 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 19 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 132 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO-) 34 mmol/L 22-29 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L 24-hour urine for calcium 2.0 mmol/24 hours 2.5-7.5 mmol/24 hours Which of the following is the most likely abnormality to be found?
explanation: Gitelman Syndrome explanations Gitelman's syndromeis caused by an SLC12A3gene mutation, which leads to a salt-losing tubulopathy because of abnormal function of the thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride transporter. Patients can present with lethargy and muscle cramps because of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Around half of patients with Gitelman's syndrome also have a long QT interval. It can be differentiated from Bartter's syndrome by the low urinary calcium excretion. Potassium supplementation is an essential part of managing the condition.

stem: A72-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with a painful skin rash characterised by large, flaccid blisters affecting a large area of the body. She has several ulcers within the mouth and these occurred a few weeks before the blisters began to appear on the body. Her only medication is amlodipine 5mg for hypertension. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is most commonly seen in elderly women and is characterised by large flaccid blisters. They particularly affect the buccal mucosa, where they rarely remain intact, and can occur in the oral cavity some weeks before they appear on the body. It is caused by anti-desmoglein immunoglobulin G autoantibodies, which lead to loss of cell-to-cell adhesion. Patients with systemic disease are managed with high-dose oral corticosteroids, which usually leads to full remission. Limited oral lesions can be managed with topical steroid therapy.

stem: A 33-year-old man who has stable ulcerative colitis managed with mesalamine presents to the Hepatology Clinic for review. His bowel symptoms are stable and he opens his bowels twice a day with normal stool, but he has been feeling increasingly tired over the past three months. He has intermittent nausea and a weight loss of 3 kg. He has one finger-breadth hepatomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 122×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine transaminase(ALT) 127 U/L 50 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 423 U/L 30-130 U/L Bilirubin 15μmol/L 21μmol/L Which of the following is the most useful next investigation for the patient's liver dysfunction?
explanation: This patient has stable ulcerative colitis but has developed an obstructive picture on liver function testing.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with three well-circumscribed areas of hair loss, two affecting the front of her scalp and one on the left temporal area. There is complete baldness of diameter 3-4cm across each area, with short 'exclamation mark'hairs around the border of the patch of hair loss. There is no evidence of inflammation or scarring. She has nail pitting. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has three discrete areas of non-scarring hair loss with exclamation mark hairs around the edge. This is characteristic of alopecia areata. The nail pitting supports the diagnosis. It is autoimmune in origin and may lead to total loss of scalp and body hair. Potent topical corticosteroids are the initial intervention of choice, although systemic immunosuppression is required for many patients.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with pain and deteriorating vision affecting her left eye, which has steadily worsened over the past 36 hours. She reports having lost colour vision at first and can now count fingers only when using her left eye. She has no past medical illnesses. The direct pupillary light reaction is diminished on the left-hand side and fundoscopy reveals a swollen optic disc. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The symptoms of an acute deterioration in vision coupled with eye pain in a young patient raises the question of acute demyelinating optic neuritis(ADON). The swollen oedematous optic disc is also consistent with the diagnosis.In ADON optic disc pallor is seen but this may take weeks to develop. Corticosteroids improve the speed of recovery in patients with ADON, but they do not impact on visual acuity in the long term. A neurology review is advised because of the risk of this being an early presentation of underlying multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with type ll diabetes and hypertension presents to the Emergency Department with nausea and lethargy over the past few days. His brother and father both have type ll diabetes and renal impairment. His blood pressure is 155/82 mmHg and heart rate 78 bpm and regular. His body mass index is 27 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most sensitive way to differentiate acute from chronic renal impairment in this case? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 320×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/ 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 385μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Chronic Kidney Disease Media explanations Serum parathyroid levels are generally lower in patients with acute renal failure versus those with chronic renal impairment. An intact parathyroid hormone(PTH) level of 170 pg/ml gives a sensitivity and specificity of around 90% for differentiating between chronic and acute renal failure. This is because a rise in PTH is seen in an attempt to maintain calcium levels in the normal range over a long time period.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with worsening shortness of breath and lethargy. He has obesity,hypertension and type lldiabetes. Examination reveals reduced chest expansion with normal breath sounds on auscultation. His body mass index is 35 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Forced expiratory volume in 1s(FEV) 82% of predicted Forced vital capacity(FVC) 81% of predicted Total lung capacity 85% of predicted Which of the following is the most probable cause of his shortness of breath?
explanation: The clinical picture seen here is consistent with obesity hypoventilation syndrome characterised by a reduction in forced vital capacity(FVC) and total lung capacity and a proportionate reduction in forced expiratory volume in 1s(FEV). Weight loss is the mainstay of intervention with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) to improve overnight oxygenation. Patients may well require surgical intervention to drive weight loss because daytime sleepiness and lethargy often limit the capacity to exercise.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with selective immunoglobulin A(IgA) deficiency is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic. She presents with a vesicular rash affecting her buttocks and upper posterior thighs, diarrhoea and weight loss over the past few months. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Anti-tissue transglutaminase is negative. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 103 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 80×10/L 150-400×109/l Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Coeliac Disease Media explanations Standard anti-tissue transglutaminase(TTG) testing is usually done for immunoglobulin A(IgA) anti-TTG antibodies. This patient has selective IgA deficiency, so, even in the face of symptoms typical of coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis, antibody testing is likely to be negative. Specific testing for lgG antibodies exists, but,in the presence of ongoing symptoms, an endoscopy with small bowel biopsy is most useful to confirm coeliac disease. A gluten exclusion diet willimprove symptoms of diarrhoea and resolve the skin rash.

stem: A45-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner complaining of frequent falls and tripping over. He has also found it increasingly hard to work in the garden because of weakness in his upper limbs and difficulty getting up. He has no significant medical illnesses and takes no regular medication. There is weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hands,tone is increased in the arm extensors and there is some fasciculation affecting the right thigh while being examined. Lower limb reflexes are diminished. Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine
explanation: This patient's gradually worsening weakness, coupled with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, fits with a potential diagnosis of motor neurone disease. Electromyography is characteristic in motor neurone disease, showing fibrillation and fasciculations. Motor units are polyphasic and have both high amplitude and long duration. Nerve conduction studies are usually also performed, which show normal sensory and motor conduction.

stem: A34-year-old woman has undergone a renal transplantation for end-stage renal failure related to typel diabetes. She has a family history of breast cancer and is worried about future risk of malignancy with immunosuppression after receiving her transplant. Which of the following cancers has the greatest rise in standardised incidence ratio after a transplantation?
explanation: Haematological malignancies are increased most in patients post-renal transplantation. A 7-to 8-fold increase in the incidence of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is seen post-transplantation and the incidence of Kaposi's sarcoma is increased up to 60-fold. This is almost certainly due to a combination of immunosuppressive regimens.

stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted for induction chemotherapy to treat acute myeloid leukaemia. He begins treatment with rasburicase to reduce the risk of acute urate nephropathy. Which of the following is the mode of action of rasburicase?
explanation: Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase that drives the metabolism of uric acid into allantoin, which is water soluble and excreted harmlessly in urine. Hydrogen peroxide is produced as a biproduct of urate oxidation. This is eliminated by endogenous antioxidants, although rasburicase is contraindicated in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is given as a once-daily 30 minutes intravenous infusion and can be used for a period of up to 7 days.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner complaining of abdominal pain with intermittent diarrhoea and constipation over the past 7 months. Her symptoms are exacerbated by eating and her abdomen is often distended. Physical examination is entirely normal, as are routine bloods. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial advice?
options: Restrict tea, coffee and alcohol consumption
explanation: General dietary advice for treatment of iritable bowel syndrome, the most likely diagnosis, here, is to increase consumption of water but reduce the consumption of drinks that may be dehydrating, such as tea, coffee and alcohol, and carbonated drinks, because they may add to bloating and abdominal pain.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department requesting help. He is hearing a third person commenting on his actions all the time and thinks that, whenever he is using his computer, his thoughts are broadcast to others in the vicinity. He is requesting that the police are called so he can be helped. He is unkempt but general physical examination is normal. Urine is weakly positive for cannabis metabolites. Which of the following is the most probable cause of his presentation?
explanation: This patient has evidence of thought broadcasting and commentary auditory hallucinations in the third person. Both are cardinal features of acute schizophrenia. It is also useful to solicit whether he has any delusional perceptions: I saw a red car at the street corner, so lknow the secret service are following me. Self-neglect is also typical of acute schizophrenia. The low-level cannabis use may well represent a degree of self-medication. An atypical antipsychotic such as risperidone is indicated for the treatment of acute symptoms.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic with swollen legs and a progressive rise in his serum creatinine. He thinks his problems began after an episode of haematuria which followed a respiratory tract infection. His blood pressure is 155/82 mmHg and he has pitting oedema of both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count 7.4×10/L 4-11×10/L (WCC) Platelets (PLT) 291×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 157 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Mesangial hypercellularity,immune complex deposition Renal biopsy staining positive for immunoglobulin A, areas of focal glomerular sclerosis Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical picture here with worsening symptoms of proteinuria, which began with haematuria after a respiratory tract infection, fits well with a diagnosis of immunoglobulin(lg)A nephropathy. The biopsy that shows that mesangial hypercellularity and IgA immune complex deposition support the diagnosis.In patients who have significant proteinuria, corticosteroids are the initial intervention of choice, with angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors used to control blood pressure and further contribute to renoprotection.

stem: A72-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and severe lethargy that have worsened significantly over the past 48 hours. She is now unable to climb the stairs. She has chronic renal impairment and started erythropoietin injections some 3 months ago, from which she initially felt great benefit. Her blood pressure is 123/82 mmHg and heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m. Which of the following is the most probable cause of her symptoms? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 71 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.9×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 398 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Ferritin 10 μg/L (300 μg/l last measured 3 months ago) 40μg/L
explanation: Anaemia of Chronic Kidney Disease explanations This patient has had a precipitous fall in her feritin levels accompanied by a rapid increase in symptoms of anaemia. Her haemoglobin(Hb) is also considerably reduced at71 g/L. This is indicative of blood loss, most probably from the gastrointestinal tract.In the absence of symptoms, a colonoscopy is potentially indicated first to rule out a right-sided colonic lesion, followed by an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, should the colonoscopy be normal. Contrast computed tomography may be considered if the patient cannot undergo endoscopic investigation.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with her husband. She has suffered two episodes of memory loss over the past three months when she has been unable to find her way home from the shops. She also has difficulties finding words and has problems with unpacking the shopping. She has hypertension but is otherwise well. Physical examination is unremarkable. Her Mini-Mental State Examination is 20/30. She is referred for a magnetic resonance imaging scan which finds atrophy of the mesial temporal lobes and temporoparietal cortical atrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are typical of Alzheimer's disease, with disorientation, memory loss and difficulty with word finding. The temporal lobe atrophy fits well with a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and her Mini- Mental State Examination is supportive of this. Three acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are available for initial treatment of Alzheimer's disease; donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine. Any of the three could be started here. Memantine can be added if the response to therapy is inadequate.

stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes a day presents to the Oncology Ward with a worsening cough and haemoptysis over the past 3-4 months. His wife is very concerned because, over the past week, he has become increasingly drowsy and confused. His blood pressure is 122/82mmHg, and heart rate is 82 bpm and regular. He has bilateral wheeze with decreased breath sounds at the left base. There are no signs of fluid overload. He is disorientated and unable to answer basic questions from the Mini-Mental State Examination. Investigations: Which of the following is the most probable cause of his symptoms? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 111 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 283×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 126 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Lung Cancer Media explanations Small-cell lung cancer is associated with smoking and usually develops in the hilar region of the lung. It is aggressive, rapidly metastases and is responsible for ectopic production of both adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) and antidiuretic hormone(ADH). In this case, the low sodium is a pointer towards the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), especially given the absence of any signs of fluid overload, or renal or hepatic dysfunction. Symptoms of SIADH resolve as treatment is instituted for the underlying lung tumour.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with chronic diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and flatulence some three weeks after returning from her honeymoon in Madagascar. She says she feels tired all the time and has lost 2-3 kg in weight. Her abdomen is mildly distended and tender on deep palpation. She has active bowel sounds. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Giardiasis is spread by water or food stuffs contaminated with faecal matter and is caused by Giardia lamblia. ALthough cases of the protozoal infection are found worldwide, it is more common where it is endemic and there is poorer sanitation. The symptoms of chronic diarrhoea with intermittent bloating and flatulence are typical of giardiasis. A single dose of tinidazole or a course of metronidazole is effective in clearing the infection. Some residual lactose intolerance may persist for a few weeks after treatment.

stem: A 74-year-old man with dementia presents to the Memory Clinic to discuss the results of his magnetic resonance scan. He is thought to have Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following proteins accumulate in Alzheimer's disease?
explanation: Tau is usually highly soluble and plays a role in microtubule stabilisation in axons. In Alzheimer's disease, tau becomes hyperphosphorylated and is then insoluble. It then aggregates to form neurofibrillary tangles. The other major component of the pathogenic lesions of Alzheimer's disease is beta-amyloid. Attempting to remove protein aggregates has been a key target of potential interventions for Alzheimer's disease.
